---
title: "Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets"
subtitle: "What it means to give every defender a receiver, why the defense keeps one man free, and how it handles stacks, stars and the receiver it fears most."
description: "Man coverage from the defense's side: Cover 1 (man-free) and its free defender (rat, robber, lurk), Cover 0 and the arithmetic of the all-out blitz, the techniques (press-man, off-man, trail) and how leverage follows the help, banjo and combo calls against stacks and bunches, brackets on a star receiver, shadow corners, when defenses choose man (third down, the red zone, talent) in nflverse charting data, and the man-beaters offenses answer with."
glossary:
  "Cover 1": {def: "Man coverage with one deep safety in the middle of the field: every eligible receiver has a defender on him, the free safety plays the deep middle as help for all of them, and the defense usually has one more defender left over to rush, spy or sit in the middle.", aliases: ["Man-free"]}
  "Cover 0": "Man coverage with no deep safety: every eligible receiver has a defender on him and no one is left to help over the top. The defenders without a man usually rush (most often a six- or seven-man blitz), though some versions keep one of them free underneath."
  Robber: {def: "A defender with no receiver to cover in man coverage (usually a safety) who sits in the middle of the field about 8 to 12 yards deep, reads the quarterback, and drives on in-breaking throws such as digs, crossers and slants. Many playbooks call him the rat, especially when he is a linebacker sitting lower, in the hole.", aliases: ["Rat"]}
  Lurk: "A free defender in man coverage, often one who lines up as a blitzer or a deep safety, who drops at the snap into the shallow middle (roughly 5 to 10 yards deep) to sit under crossing routes and hot throws. A disguised cousin of the robber."
  Banjo: "A two-defender rule for two receivers who line up close together (a stack, a bunch or a tight split): instead of each defender locking onto one man, they decide at the release, usually with the outside defender taking the first receiver to break outside and the inside defender the first to break inside (an in/out banjo; some teams split them short/deep instead), so neither has to fight through traffic."
  "Combo coverage": "Any coverage in which two or more defenders share two or more receivers and decide who takes whom by how the routes declare after the snap (a banjo is the simplest), or which mixes man rules and zone rules on the same snap. Charters also use the word for a play that fits no single coverage label."
  Bracket: "Two defenders on one receiver, one on each side of him: underneath and over the top (under-over) or inside and outside (in-out), so that whichever way he breaks, a defender is already there. The usual way to take away a star."
  "Shadow corner": "A cornerback assigned to follow one receiver (usually the opponent's best) wherever he lines up, left, right or in the slot, instead of staying on one side of the field."
  "Inside help": "A defender positioned toward the middle of the field from a man defender (the deep middle safety, or a robber underneath) who can take routes that break inside, so the man defender can play outside leverage and take away the sideline."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
#| output: false
import os
import logging
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import animation
from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, routes as r, style, draw_marker

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
READ_GREEN = "#0f7a55"          # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text and read lines
OD, DD = style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.DEFENSE_DARK
LINE_D, OFF_BALL, GUN = -0.7, -1.5, -5.0
LOS = 40                        # the offense's own 30: room for deep routes in the window
FW = 160 / 3


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- players and alignments
def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=key if label is None else label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line5():
    """Five offensive linemen, 1.6 yards apart (only the center is lettered)."""
    return [O(k, k, LINE_D, w, "C" if k == "C" else "") for k, w in
            (("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2))]


def spread(rb_w=2.0, x_w=-15.0, h_w=-9.0, y_w=9.0, z_w=15.0):
    """11 personnel, shotgun 2x2: X and Z on the line (with the five linemen, seven on the line);
    H in the left slot and Y, a tight end split out, in the right slot, both a step off the ball."""
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, rb_w, "R"),
                      O("X", "WR", LINE_D, x_w), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, h_w),
                      O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, y_w), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, z_w)]


def dline():
    """Four down linemen (a four-man rush), strength to the offense's right."""
    return [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"),
            D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")]


def moved(players, extra=None):
    extra = extra or {}
    return [q.moved(d=extra[q.key][0], w=extra[q.key][1]) if q.key in extra else q for q in players]


def cover1_def(extra=None):
    """Nickel Cover 1 against 2x2: corners pressed with a slight outside shade (their help is
    inside), the nickel ($) on H, the strong safety on the tight end, the Will on the back, the
    Mike free, the free safety alone in the deep middle."""
    return moved(dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 2.4, "W"),
                            D("NB", "NB", 4.0, -9.8, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 9.8, "SS"),
                            D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.9, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.9, "CB"),
                            D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0, "FS")], extra)


def zero_front():
    """Six at the line for an all-out pressure: four linemen widened a little, and both linebackers
    walked up into the A gaps beside the center (a 'double A-gap mug')."""
    return [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.8, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -3.0, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 3.0, "T"),
            D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.8, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.4, -0.95, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.4, 0.95, "W")]


def protect(p, rushers=("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"), linemen=("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")):
    """Linemen set, rushers engage them: enough to say 'pass', no more."""
    for k in linemen:
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    for k in rushers:
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)


def route_to(p, key, *pts, delay=0.0, speed=None):
    """A route through absolute (d, w) points."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    return p.route(key, [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in pts], frame="field", delay=delay, speed=speed)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drawing helpers
def P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def clean(ax):
    """Drop the painted yard numbers (they sit where receivers stand); clip all text to the window."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def ruler(fld, p, fs=6.0, step=5, top=30):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) just inside the left edge of the window."""
    xl = FW - fld.y1 + 0.4
    for d in range(step, top + 1, step):
        y = p.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 1.5 <= y <= fld.x1 - 1.5:
            fld.ax.text(xl, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == step else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                        ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def draw(p, width_in=8.3, ax=None, show_ruler=True, **kw):
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, title=False, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    if show_ruler:
        ruler(fld, p)
    return fld


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True):
    x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13,
                fontweight=weight, linespacing=1.15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9) if box else None)


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, ha="center"):
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = P(fld, p, *text_at), P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13, linespacing=1.15,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=7),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def branch(fld, p, pts, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.5, dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow", z=5):
    """A path through absolute (d, w) points: by default a defender's reaction (orange dashes)."""
    xs, ys = P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=z, solid_capstyle="round")
    if end == "arrow":
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=z))


def oval(fld, p, center, size, color=style.DEFENSE, label=None, alpha=0.13, fs=7.0, ls=(0, (3, 2))):
    """A shaded area (depth, width) with an optional italic label at its centre."""
    x, y = P(fld, p, *center)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), size[1], size[0], fc=color, alpha=alpha, ec=color, lw=0.9,
                             ls=ls, zorder=1.6))
    if label:
        fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                    style="italic", zorder=3)


def vdim(fld, p, w, d0, d1, text, fs=6.5, side=1):
    """A vertical dimension line at width w from depth d0 to d1, labelled beside it."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(fld, p, d0, w), P(fld, p, d1, w)
    fld.ax.annotate("", (float(x1), float(y1)), xytext=(float(x0), float(y0)),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8), zorder=6)
    say(fld, p, (d0 + d1) / 2, w + side * 2.4, text, fontsize=fs)


def hline(fld, p, d, w0, w1, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (4, 3))):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(fld, p, d, w0), P(fld, p, d, w1)
    fld.ax.plot([float(x0), float(x1)], [float(y0), float(y1)], color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=2.5)


def number(fld, p, keys_texts, dd=-2.9):
    """Receiver numbers (#1, #2 ...) under the named receivers."""
    for key, txt in keys_texts:
        q = p.players[key]
        say(fld, p, q.d + dd, q.w, txt, color=OD, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")


def panel_title(ax, text, fs=8.6):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=fs, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


def under_note(ax, text, fs=6.9):
    ax.text(0.5, -0.02, text, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=fs, color=style.INK,
            linespacing=1.2)


LEGEND = {
    "route": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.8, label="route"),
    "man": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (1, 2)), label="man assignment"),
    "drop": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="defender's drop / path"),
    "motion": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2.2)), label="pre-snap motion"),
    "react": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2.2)), label="defender's reaction"),
    "rush": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8, label="rusher"),
    "ring": Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=11, mfc="none", mec=style.THIRD, mew=2, label="player to watch"),
    "area": Patch(fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.2, ec=style.DEFENSE, label="area a defender guards"),
    "ltg": Line2D([], [], color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=2.2, label="line to gain"),
    "pass": Line2D([], [], color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), label="the throw"),
}


def field_legend(ax, keys, fs=7.0, ncol=None):
    hs = [LEGEND[k] for k in keys]
    ax.legend(handles=hs, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=ncol or min(len(hs), 4),
              fontsize=fs, frameon=False, handlelength=2.0, columnspacing=1.2, borderaxespad=0.2)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- motion: keyframes, frame strips, video
def set_tracks(p, tracks, t_end=None):
    """Hand-made keyframes {key: [(t, d, w), ...]} for some players, after all routes are added.
    gridiron's man() keeps a shrinking cushion that ends on top of the receiver (which hides him in
    print) and cannot switch receivers, so man defenders here are keyframed by hand."""
    kf, t0, t1 = p._compile()
    kf = dict(kf)
    for key, rows in tracks.items():
        q = p.players[key]
        rows = [(min(t0, -1.0), q.d, q.w), (0.0, q.d, q.w)] + [tuple(r_) for r_ in rows]
        kf[key] = np.array(rows, dtype=float)
    p._compiled = (kf, t0, max(t1, t_end or 0.0, *[rows[-1][0] for rows in tracks.values()]))


def chase(p, key, target, off, lag=0.25, t_on=0.7, t_end=3.6, t_start=0.1):
    """Keyframes for a man defender who settles `off` = (down, toward the offense's right) yards
    from where his receiver was `lag` seconds earlier."""
    q = p.players[key]
    rows = []
    for tt in np.round(np.arange(t_start, t_end, 0.05), 3):
        f = min(1.0, max(0.0, (tt - t_start) / (t_on - t_start)))
        f = f * f * (3 - 2 * f)
        tgt = p.position(target, max(0.0, tt - lag)) + np.array(off)
        rows.append((tt, *(np.array([q.d, q.w]) * (1 - f) + tgt * f)))
    return rows


def ease(points, step=0.05):
    """Smooth keyframes through (t, d, w) waypoints (ease in and out on each leg)."""
    rows = []
    for (ta, da, wa), (tb, db, wb) in zip(points[:-1], points[1:]):
        for tt in np.arange(ta, tb, step):
            f = (tt - ta) / (tb - ta)
            f = f * f * (3 - 2 * f)
            rows.append((round(float(tt), 3), da + (db - da) * f, wa + (wb - wa) * f))
    rows.append(tuple(points[-1]))
    return rows


def frame(ax, p, t, lateral, window, rings=(), ltg=True):
    """Everyone at time t, with faint trails of where they have been and the ball's flight so far."""
    ylo, yhi = sorted((p.ball_y - lateral[0], p.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=p.los, window=window, numbers=False, lateral=(ylo, yhi),
                to_go=p.to_go if ltg else None)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    wl, wr = sorted(lateral)
    ring = dict(rings)
    for k, q in p.players.items():
        d, w = p.position(k, t)
        if not (window[0] + 0.4 < d < window[1] - 0.4 and wl + 0.4 < w < wr - 0.4):
            continue
        if t > 0:
            pts = np.array([p.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(0.0, t, 40)])
            if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) > 0.3:
                xs, ys = P(fld, p, pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
                ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if q.side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0,
                        alpha=0.5, zorder=3)
        x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
        draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), q.side, q.label, ppy, ring=ring.get(k))
    for kind, to, te in p.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass" and t > te:
            ts = np.linspace(te, t, 20)
            b = np.array([p.ball_position(tt) for tt in ts])
            xs, ys = P(fld, p, b[:, 0], b[:, 1])
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9)
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(xs[-1]) - 0.9, float(ys[-1])), 1.0, 0.62, fc=style.BALL, ec="white",
                                 lw=0.5, zorder=11))
    clean(ax)
    return fld


def strip_grid(p, times, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=6.5, deco=None, fs=6.9):
    """Print stand-in for an animation: numbered panels, each with a sentence underneath."""
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    ph = pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0])
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False, figsize=(width_in, nrows * (ph + 0.75)))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        fld = frame(ax, p, t, lateral, window, rings)
        if deco:
            deco(i, fld, p)
        panel_title(ax, f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"+{t:.1f} s"))
        under_note(ax, notes[i], fs=fs)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=3.2, w_pad=0.8)
    return fig


def strip_rows(plays, names, times, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), width_in=6.5, fs=6.6, deco=None):
    """One row per play, one column per moment: two versions of a play on the same clock."""
    nc = len(times)
    pw = width_in / nc
    ph = pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0])
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(plays), nc, squeeze=False, figsize=(width_in, len(plays) * (ph + 0.8)))
    for i, (p, nm) in enumerate(zip(plays, names)):
        for j, t in enumerate(times):
            fld = frame(axes[i, j], p, t, lateral, window, rings)
            if deco:
                deco(i, j, fld, p)
            panel_title(axes[i, j], f"{nm}: " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"+{t:.1f} s"), fs=8)
            under_note(axes[i, j], notes[i][j], fs=fs)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=3.0, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(plays, names, lateral, window, t_end, rings=(), width_in=6.0, t_start=-0.4):
    """Web version: the plays side by side, on one clock."""
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    n = len(plays)
    span_w, span_d = abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]), window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n, figsize=(width_in, width_in / n * span_d / span_w + 0.5), squeeze=False)
    ts = np.round(np.arange(t_start, t_end + 1e-9, 0.1), 2)

    def update(i):
        for ax, p, nm in zip(axes[0], plays, names):
            ax.clear()
            frame(ax, p, max(0.0, float(ts[i])), lateral, window, rings)
            panel_title(ax, (nm + ": " if nm else "") + ("snap" if ts[i] <= 0 else f"+{ts[i]:.1f} s"), fs=9)
        return []

    fig.tight_layout()
    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=100, blit=False)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (nflverse coverage labels joined to play-by-play, 2018–2025)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = list(range(2018, 2026))
PB_COLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "down", "ydstogo", "yardline_100", "defteam",
           "qb_dropback", "sack", "yards_gained"]
_pb = pbp(SEASONS, columns=PB_COLS)
_pb = _pb[_pb["season_type"] == "REG"]
_part = (nfl().load_participation(SEASONS).to_pandas()
         .rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})
         [["game_id", "play_id", "defense_coverage_type", "number_of_pass_rushers", "time_to_throw"]])
CV = _pb.merge(_part, on=["game_id", "play_id"])
# charted dropbacks; blown coverages, 'combo' and prevent left out
CV = CV[(CV["qb_dropback"] == 1) & CV["defense_coverage_type"].notna()
        & ~CV["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["BLOWN", "COMBO", "PREVENT"])].copy()
CV["man"] = CV["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["COVER_0", "COVER_1", "2_MAN"])
CV["c0"] = CV["defense_coverage_type"].eq("COVER_0")
CV["era"] = np.where(CV["season"] <= 2022, "2018–2022 (NGS charting)", "2023–2025 (FTN charting)")
CV["explosive"] = CV["yards_gained"] >= 20
CV["rush5"] = CV["number_of_pass_rushers"] >= 5


def _dd(row):
    if row.down == 1:
        return "1st down"
    if row.down == 2:
        return "2nd down"
    for hi, lab in ((2, "3rd/4th & 1–2"), (6, "3rd/4th & 3–6"), (10, "3rd/4th & 7–10")):
        if row.ydstogo <= hi:
            return lab
    return "3rd/4th & 11+"


CV["dd"] = CV.apply(_dd, axis=1)
CV["zone_fp"] = pd.cut(CV["yardline_100"], [0, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 100],
                       labels=["1–5", "6–10", "11–20", "21–40", "41–80", "81–99"])
SEASON_MAN = CV.groupby("season")["man"].mean() * 100
TEAM = CV.groupby(["season", "defteam"])[["man", "c0"]].mean().reset_index()
TEAM["man_rank"] = TEAM.groupby("season")["man"].rank(ascending=False, method="min")
TEAM["c0_rank"] = TEAM.groupby("season")["c0"].rank(ascending=False, method="min")
```

Third-and-5 in the red zone. The offense comes out with two receivers on each side, and as the
quarterback starts his cadence the broadcast's camera catches something it rarely shows on first
down: both cornerbacks walk up until they are standing a yard from the receivers' faces, squared
up, eyes on the receivers' belts rather than on the quarterback. The slot receiver motions across
the formation, and a defender jogs across with him, mirroring every step. One safety drifts back
to the middle of the field, 14 yards deep, all alone. The analyst says, "They're in man." The ball
is snapped, the quarterback looks to his favourite target running a crossing route, and a
linebacker who had been standing in the middle covering nobody steps into the lane and knocks the
ball down. Who was that linebacker covering? Nobody, and that was the point. This chapter is about
the coverages in which defenders cover *people*: what each defender is asked to do, the one or two
defenders the system deliberately leaves free, and the tricks defenses use when one-on-one isn't
enough.

**You'll be able to…**

- Draw Cover 1 (man-free), its robber and rat versions, and Cover 0, and say for each one who
  covers whom, who is left free, and what the defense gives up.
- Tell press-man, off-man and trail technique apart on a replay, and explain why a man defender's
  leverage depends on where his help is.
- Recognise a banjo against stacked and bunched receivers, a bracket on a star receiver, and a
  shadow cornerback, and say what each costs the rest of the coverage.
- Predict when a defense is most likely to play man (third down, the red zone, a great cornerback)
  and read the situational numbers that show it.
- Name the offense's standard answers to man coverage (rubs and mesh, slants, double moves,
  motion, a back on a linebacker) and the defensive counter to each.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **Zones, technique words and the shell** ([Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)):
  [press](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-press) is a defender lined up within a yard or two of a
  receiver to jam him; [off coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-coverage) starts 5 to 10
  yards away; the [cushion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cushion) is that gap.
  [Trail technique](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trail-technique) is running just behind and
  underneath a receiver, trusting a safety over the top. The middle of the field is
  [closed](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofc) (MOFC) when a safety stands deep in it and
  [open](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofo) (MOFO) when no one does. The
  [hole](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hole-zone) is the middle of the field about 8 to 15 yards
  deep, in front of the deep safety. The 5-yard contact rule, and the "Mel Blount" and "Ty Law" rules
  behind it, are there too. Coverage numbers (Cover 0 to Cover 9) mostly count the deep
  defenders.
- **Man and zone, one-high and two-high** ([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)):
  in [man coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage) each defender follows one
  receiver; in [zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-coverage) each guards an area. A
  [one-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-high) shell has one deep safety, a
  [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) shell two. A
  [blitz](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-blitz) sends five or more rushers. The
  [nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nickel) package has five defensive backs; the fifth,
  the nickel back, is drawn as **$**.
- **Leverage and press from the receiver's side** ([The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd)):
  a defender's [leverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside) is the side of
  the receiver he lines up on; a receiver beats press with his
  [release](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-release-vs-press); a
  [double move](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move) fakes one route and runs another.
  Within five yards of the line an NFL defender may jam a receiver; beyond that, contact before the
  throw is [illegal contact](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-illegal-contact).
- **Man-beaters** ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)):
  [mesh](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mesh) crosses two receivers over the middle; a
  [rub route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rub-route) makes a chasing defender go around a
  teammate; the [angle route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-angle-route) puts a running back
  on a linebacker.
- **Motion** ([Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)):
  a defender who [travels](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-travel-man-defender-follows-motion)
  across the formation with a man in motion suggests man coverage; an
  [exchange](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-exchange-man-coverage-on-motion) is a man defense
  swapping receivers instead.
- **Formations** ([Spread Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)):
  [2x2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2x2) is two receivers on each side,
  [3x1](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3x1) three and one, [empty](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-empty)
  has no back in the backfield. In a [stack](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stack) one receiver
  lines up directly behind another; a [bunch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bunch) is three in a
  tight cluster. Receivers are numbered from the sideline in: #1 is the widest on his side.

*Reading the diagrams:* offense is blue circles (X, Y, Z, H receivers; Q quarterback; R running
back; C center). Defense is outlined squares: E and T the defensive ends and tackles, M the Mike
(middle) linebacker, W the Will, **$** the nickel back, CB a cornerback, FS and SS the free and
strong safety. Dotted orange lines join a man defender to the receiver he covers; dashed orange
arrows are defenders' movements; shaded ovals are areas a defender guards. A green ring marks the
player to watch. The small numbers down the left edge give the depth in yards past the line of
scrimmage (the darker blue line); the orange line is the line to gain.
:::

## What man coverage asks of a defender

Every pass defense has to answer one question before the snap: when the receivers start running,
how does each defender know what to do? Zone coverage answers with *places*: you have the deep
third, you have the flat, guard it and take whoever comes. Man coverage answers with *people*:
you have number 11, go where he goes. Everything in this chapter grows from that one choice, so it
is worth slowing down on what it buys and what it costs.

What it buys is **tightness and certainty**. A zone defender guards grass, so a receiver can sit
down in the soft spot between two zones and catch the ball with nobody within three yards of him.
A man defender guards a body. If he is good enough, there is no soft spot, because the soft spot
moves with the receiver and so does the defender. There is also no confusion about who takes the
receiver who wanders between two areas, which is where zone coverages break down. And man coverage
lets a defense choose its matchups: its best cornerback on their best receiver, its fastest
linebacker on their running back.

What it costs comes from where the man defender is looking. A zone defender watches the
quarterback and can break on the ball the moment it's thrown. A man defender watches his receiver,
usually his hips and belt, because that is where a route's direction shows first. So he often
has his **back to the quarterback**. He doesn't see the ball leave the hand; he reacts to the
receiver's hands and eyes going up. He can't help a teammate, because his own man would be left
alone. If the quarterback escapes the pocket and runs, half the defense is running *away* from him,
following receivers downfield. And if a receiver beats his defender, by a quick release, a sharp
break, or a route that drags the defender into traffic, there is nobody nearby to fix it.

That last problem is the one man coverages are built around. The pure version, every defender on a
receiver and nobody else, is all risk: one lost footrace is a touchdown. So almost every man
coverage keeps one or two defenders **free**, with no receiver of their own, to help the others.
Where the free defenders stand, how many there are, and what they do give us the family names:
Cover 1, Cover 0, the robber and rat versions, brackets. The free defender is the whole game.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Man coverage exists because **a defender who covers a person never has to decide whose person
he is.** Against short, precise throws (the slant, the stick, the quick out) a zone defender is
often a step too far away, because he started in the middle of an area. A man defender starts
on the receiver and stays there, and that tightness is worth most where throws are short and
timing is everything: third-and-short, the red zone, any down where the defense is also sending
extra rushers. The price is eyes: man defenders watch receivers, not the ball, and need help
somewhere behind them.
:::

### A little history: the bump-and-run, and the rules that answered it

Man coverage is as old as the forward pass, but the modern, aggressive form grew up in the 1960s
American Football League. Willie Brown, a cornerback who had been a linebacker in college, began
jamming receivers right at the line in 1963, and with Al Davis's Raiders he became the face of
**bump-and-run**: line up in the receiver's face, hit him at the snap, then run with him. (Davis
modelled the Raiders' version on the full-court press of John Wooden's UCLA basketball teams.)
Brown played 12 seasons in Oakland and is in the Hall of Fame.[^bumprun]

The rules answered twice (the 1978 "Mel Blount rule" and the 2004 "Ty Law rule", both told in
[Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd); the Ty Law game is in this chapter's film
room). For man coverage the result is the shape of the modern craft. Inside five yards it is a
fight of hands and feet; beyond five yards, until the ball is thrown, the defender may not initiate
contact that impedes the receiver, so everything depends on *position*: being on the right side of
the receiver, at the right distance, before he breaks.[^contact] Physical man coverage followed by a
rules response is a pattern you'll see again in
[Contact Rules and Penalties](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).

## Cover 1: man-free

The most common man coverage in football is
[**Cover 1**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-1), which coaches also call
[**man-free**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-free). The name is the coverage: man coverage
on every eligible receiver, plus one *free* safety who has no man at all and plays the deep middle
of the field. The "1" is the one deep defender.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cover1-2x2
#| fig-cap: "Cover 1 against a 2x2 formation (11 personnel: one back, one tight end, three wide receivers), third-and-7. Every eligible receiver has a man defender (dotted lines): the cornerbacks (CB) on the outside receivers X and Z, the nickel back ($) on the slot H, the strong safety (SS) on the tight end Y, the Will (W) on the running back. The free safety (FS, ringed) has nobody: he guards the deep middle for all of them. That still leaves one defender over, the Mike (M, ringed), who here drops into the hole, the middle of the field underneath, as a spare helper (a job with its own names, coming up below). The corners line up a step outside their receivers, because their help is inside."
p = Play(spread(), cover1_def(), los=LOS, to_go=7)
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, -0.5), zone=(3.6, 9.0), label="hole")
p.zone((17.5, 0.0), (6.5, 26.0), label="deep middle")
protect(p)
p.highlight("FS", "MIKE")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 22.5))
say(fld, p, 14.0, 7.8, "FS: no man.\nHelp for everyone", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 10.6, -10.0, "the spare defender: sits,\nrushes or spies", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -3.8, -19.6, "outside shade:\nhelp is inside", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -3.8, 19.6, "outside shade:\nhelp is inside", fontsize=6.8)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["man", "drop", "area", "ltg"])
plt.show()
```

Count the defenders in the picture. Four rush. The offense has five eligible receivers, so five
defenders have a man. That is nine. The tenth is the free safety, alone in the middle 13 to 15
yards deep, and the eleventh, here the Mike linebacker, is free too. Cover 1 against five
receivers and a four-man rush always leaves that eleventh man over, and the defense gets to decide
what to do with him. He can rush, making it a five-man pressure; he can sit in the middle as a
helper; or he can mirror a running quarterback (a [spy](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spy),
covered in [Third Down](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd)). The section on the free
defender below is about that choice.

The free safety's own job sounds impossible at first: one man "helping" on five receivers. He
doesn't try to cover them all. He starts in the middle, 13 to 15 yards deep, reads the
quarterback's eyes and shoulders, and works toward the deepest route breaking *inside* or straight
up the middle, the throws a corner with outside leverage can't reach. Routes to the sideline are
the corners' problem. Two deep routes into the middle at once (two posts, or a post and a seam)
are his nightmare, for the same reason a high-low is the robber's below: one man, two targets.
How common is all this? In the public charting, Cover 1 was the label on roughly a quarter to a
third of charted NFL dropbacks in every season from 2018 to 2025, by far the most of any man
coverage.[^c1share]

### Who takes whom

A man coverage is only as good as its matching rules, because the offense chooses the formation
and the defense has to sort itself out in the 15 or so seconds before the snap. A typical set of
rules, which varies by team:

- **Corners take the widest receiver on each side (#1).** They are the best man-to-man athletes on
  the field and the outside receivers are usually the fastest.
- **The nickel takes the slot receiver** (#2 to his side); in a base defense, with no nickel back,
  that job goes to a safety or a linebacker.
- **A safety or linebacker takes the tight end**, matched for size.
- **A linebacker takes the running back**, and if the back stays in to block, that linebacker
  is free to rush the quarterback (a "hug" or "green-dog" rule) or drop into the middle.
- **The free safety takes nobody** and plays the deep middle.

These are starting rules, and the call can rearrange them. If the plan is for the strong safety to
come down and *rob* (the next big section), he can't also cover the tight end, so a linebacker
takes the tight end instead, and the spare defender moves up from the linebacker level to the
safety level. The count never changes: five receivers need five men, and whoever is left over is
the free defender.

The rules have to cope with whatever the offense shows. When a receiver motions across the
formation, his defender either *travels* with him, the classic tell you met in
[Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd), or the
defenders *exchange*, each sliding over a spot and swapping receivers. When the offense shows three
receivers to one side, someone from the other side has to be matched across. When the offense
lines up in a formation the defense didn't prepare for, the defense has a short list of simple
"checks" to fall back on. Much of what looks like a cornerback getting "beat" on a broadcast is
actually two defenders who disagreed about a rule.

### The help is inside, so the leverage is outside

Look again at the cornerbacks in the figure: each is a step *outside* his receiver. That isn't a
style choice; it follows from where the help is. In Cover 1 the free safety lives in the deep
middle, and often a second free defender sits underneath in the middle too. That help is
**[inside help](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-inside-help)**: defenders positioned toward the
middle of the field from the man defender, who can get to routes that break inside (posts, digs,
slants) faster than they can get to the sideline.

So the man defender takes away the side where help can't reach him. A cornerback with inside help
plays **outside leverage**: he protects the sideline routes (the fade, the out, the comeback) and,
in coaches' language, *funnels* the receiver inside, toward the help. If the receiver runs a post,
the corner chases and the free safety arrives from the middle. If he runs a slant or a dig, the
corner trails and the help underneath is waiting. The general rule, which works for every man
coverage in this chapter: **play away from your help**. Where there is help, you can give ground;
where there isn't, you can't.

That is the starting rule, not a law, and coaches bend it in three common ways:

- **Split.** A receiver who lines up close to the sideline has very little room outside him, so
  the sideline itself is a kind of help, and his defender often plays *inside* leverage instead.
  A receiver with a tight split, near the formation, has room both ways and gets the outside
  shade.
- **Down and distance.** On third-and-short many Cover 1 teams press head-up or with an inside
  shade to take away the slant, the fastest way to the sticks, and accept the fade, a slower,
  harder throw the free safety couldn't reach anyway.
- **The slot.** A slot receiver has room to break either way (a "two-way go"), and his defender
  often shades inside: the inside break is the quick throw, while a break outside means a longer
  throw toward the sideline that gives him time to recover.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: Cover 1"}
Cover 1 is the compromise that makes man coverage affordable. Pure man everywhere leaves every
defender alone against a deep route. One deep safety turns every one-on-one into a
one-on-one *with help on the deep, inside throw*, and the coverage still has a defender left over
to rush or to rob. It keeps the box strong, too. Only one safety lives deep; the other plays
close to the line of scrimmage, on the tight end or as the spare, so with the linebackers the
defense still has seven or eight players near the line to stop the run. (Against a run, a man
defender whose receiver blocks him becomes a run defender; who takes what in the run game is the
subject of [Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).)
**What it gives up:** the middle of the field
underneath (unless the extra defender sits there), the receiver who simply wins his matchup to the
outside, where there is no help, and the throws that make man defenders run through traffic.
:::

## Press, off and trail: the man defender's techniques

"Man coverage" says *who*; technique says *how*. The same Cover 1 call can be played with every
cornerback in the receivers' faces or with every cornerback seven yards off, and the difference
changes which throws are open. There are three basic ways to cover a man.

```{python}
#| label: fig-techniques
#| fig-cap: "Three ways to play man on the same receiver (X, on the offense's left; simulated). Blue is the route, orange dashes the cornerback's movement. 1. Press-man: the corner starts a yard away, jams X inside the five-yard limit (dashed line), then runs on his hip on a go route. 2. Off-man: the corner starts about seven yards off with a cushion, backpedals while X pushes upfield, and drives on the curl when X stops; he can see the break coming but arrives a step late, conceding the short throw. 3. Trail: the corner presses, then runs a step behind and underneath X on a post, protecting the low throw, because a safety (FS) is over the top to take the high one."
LAT_T, WIN_T = (-23.5, -6.5), (-3.5, 20.0)


def tech_panel(ax, kind):
    off = [O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0)]
    dfn = []
    if kind == "press":
        dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 1.0, -14.4, "CB")]
    elif kind == "off":
        dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 7.0, -14.0, "CB")]
    else:
        dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 1.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 16.5, -8.6, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    if kind == "press":
        route_to(p, "X", (18.5, -15.3))
    elif kind == "off":
        route_to(p, "X", (12.6, -15.0), (11.2, -13.7))
    else:
        route_to(p, "X", (9.5, -15.0), (17.0, -10.8))
    p.highlight("CB")
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT_T, window=WIN_T, title=False)
    clean(ax)
    ruler(fld, p, fs=5.5)
    if kind == "press":
        hline(fld, p, 5.0, -19.8, -8.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
        say(fld, p, 5.9, -10.3, "5 yd: contact\nmust stop", fontsize=6.0)
        branch(fld, p, [(1.0, -14.4), (2.4, -14.5), (5.0, -14.4), (17.0, -14.3)])
        say(fld, p, 2.4, -11.9, "jam", fontsize=6.4, color=DD, weight="bold")
    elif kind == "off":
        # backpedal while X pushes upfield, then drive downhill on the curl from above it
        branch(fld, p, [(7.0, -14.0), (10.8, -14.1), (12.4, -13.3), (11.8, -13.0)])
        vdim(fld, p, -11.0, 0.0, 6.6, "cushion\n~7 yd", fs=6.0)
        say(fld, p, 15.5, -14.0, "sees the break,\narrives late", fontsize=6.0)
    else:
        branch(fld, p, [(1.0, -15.8), (3.0, -15.9), (8.4, -15.9), (14.6, -12.2)])
        say(fld, p, 12.0, -8.9, "help over\nthe top", fontsize=6.0)
        say(fld, p, 12.5, -19.6, "a step behind,\nunderneath", fontsize=6.0)
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.45))
for ax, kind, ttl in zip(axes, ("press", "off", "trail"), ("1. Press-man", "2. Off-man", "3. Trail")):
    tech_panel(ax, kind)
    panel_title(ax, ttl)
fig.legend(handles=[LEGEND["route"], LEGEND["react"], LEGEND["ring"]], loc="upper center",
           bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.04), ncol=3, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8, rect=(0, 0.05, 1, 1))
plt.show()
```

**Press-man** is the bump-and-run's descendant. The defender lines up within a yard or two of the
receiver, gets his hands on him at the snap (legal inside five yards), and tries to knock him off
his path and onto the defender's terms. If the jam lands, the route is late, and a late route in
a timing offense is a dead route: the quarterback's feet have finished their drop and the receiver
isn't where he's supposed to be. If the jam misses, the defender has to turn and run with a
receiver who now has a step on him. Press-man is the purest test of athletes in football, and the
reason teams pay elite cornerbacks: hips that turn fast, long arms, and the recovery speed to
survive a miss. You met the receiver's side of this fight in
[The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd).

**Off-man** gives the receiver room. The defender starts 5 to 8 yards away, often with his weight
back, and backpedals or shuffles as the receiver comes toward him, keeping that **cushion** while
he reads the route. Off-man trades the jam for vision: he sees the break coming and is rarely
beaten deep. The cost is the short throw. A receiver who turns around at six yards against a
defender who started at seven is open, and good quarterbacks take that throw all day. Off-man is
common against very fast receivers, against receivers in the slot (where a jam is harder because
the receiver can release either way), and on long-yardage downs where a six-yard catch doesn't
hurt.

**Trail technique** is what man defenders do when they have help over the top. The defender runs a
step behind the receiver and slightly underneath him, on his hip, taking away anything thrown low
or short, and trusts a safety to take the ball thrown high and deep. It is the technique of
[2-Man](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2-man), two deep safeties with man underneath
([Cover 2 and Tampa 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)), and of any Cover 1 defender whose man
runs into the free safety's area. Trailing looks like losing on a broadcast (the receiver is
ahead), but the trailing defender is exactly where he wants to be: under the throw. To tell
trailing from being beaten on a replay, look for the safety. If one is arriving over the top, the
corner is trailing on purpose; if nobody is coming, he has simply been beaten.

Whatever the technique, everything ends at the catch point, and there the key idea is **phase**.
A defender who is *in phase* is on the receiver's hip, stride for stride, close enough to turn his
head, find the ball and play it as if he were the receiver. A defender who is *out of phase*, a
step or more behind, can't afford to turn and look, because he'd lose more ground. So he watches
the receiver instead and plays his **hands**: when the receiver's eyes widen and his hands come up,
the ball is arriving, and the defender rips through the hands as they close. That is what "he
reacts to the receiver's hands" meant earlier. It is also where pass interference lives. Once the
ball is thrown, a defender who contacts a receiver more than a yard past the line and significantly
hinders his chance to catch it commits pass interference, unless he is playing the ball himself.
Not turning around is not a foul in itself, but a defender who isn't looking for the ball is not
"playing the ball", so any contact before it arrives is likely to draw the flag.[^dpi] The details
are in [Contact Rules and Penalties](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).

Teams rarely pick one technique for a whole game. They pick per matchup and per call: press on
a slow receiver, off on a fast one; press on third-and-2, off on third-and-14. The quarterback's
pre-snap read is partly a read of these techniques, which is why defenses mix them and sometimes
show press and bail out at the snap.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"Press means man, off means zone."** As [Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)
warned, alignment alone doesn't tell you; plenty of man calls are played off, and plenty of zone
corners press and bail. The man-coverage tell to add is the defender's stance and angle before
the snap: a man defender is usually squared up to his receiver and slightly turned toward the
sideline; a zone corner is usually turned in so he can see the quarterback.
:::

## The free defender: rat, robber and lurk

Back to the eleventh man. In Cover 1 with a four-man rush, one defender has no receiver and no
deep responsibility. Defenses can turn him into a fifth rusher (Cover 1 pressure, in
[Blitzing](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd)) or keep him in coverage as a
helper. As a helper he has three common names, and coaches don't use them identically, so
learn the jobs rather than the words. On broadcasts you'll hear the whole call named after him:
"Cover 1 Robber," "Cover 1 Rat," "Cover 1 Hole." The figure shows the choices one at a time, and
notice that each one changes who covers the tight end and the back.

```{python}
#| label: fig-free-player
#| fig-cap: "Four ways to use the spare defender in Cover 1, one per panel (a defense picks one per snap; the corners on X and Z, wide of the frame, are the same in all four). 1. Rat: the Mike (M), with no man, drops into the low hole, about 5 to 8 yards deep, under crossing routes. 2. Robber: the safeties start two-high; at the snap the free safety spins to the deep middle and the strong safety (SS) comes down to 8 to 12 yards to drive on digs and deep crossers, so the Mike has to take the tight end Y. 3. Lurk: the Will (W) walks up as if to blitz and drops out at the snap into the shallow middle, where the quarterback's hot throw is supposed to go; the Mike takes the back. 4. Or the spare man rushes: Cover 1 pressure, with five rushers. Each version changes who covers Y and the back, but the count is the same: five receivers, five men."
LAT_F, WIN_F = (-13.5, 13.5), (-7.0, 17.5)


def free_panel(ax, kind):
    extra, keys = {}, [("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")]
    if kind == "robber":
        extra = {"FS": (13.0, -7.0), "SS": (13.0, 7.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 6.0), "WILL": (4.5, 1.2)}
        keys = [("NB", "H"), ("MIKE", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")]
    elif kind == "lurk":
        extra = {"WILL": (1.3, -7.6), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.6)}
        keys = [("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("MIKE", "RB")]
    p = Play(spread(), cover1_def(extra=extra), los=LOS, to_go=None)
    for d_, t_ in keys:
        p.man(d_, t_)
    free = {"rat": "MIKE", "robber": "SS", "lurk": "WILL", "rush": "MIKE"}[kind]
    p.highlight(free)
    if kind == "rush":
        p.rush("MIKE", pts=[(-3.5, 2.6), (-8.0, 2.4)])
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT_F, window=WIN_F, title=False)
    clean(ax)
    ruler(fld, p, fs=5.5)
    if kind == "rat":
        oval(fld, p, (6.6, -0.6), (3.0, 6.5), label="hole", fs=6.0)
        branch(fld, p, [(4.5, -1.8), (6.0, -0.9)], lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, 10.2, -7.6, "M has no man:\nsits low, eyes on Q", fontsize=6.0)
    elif kind == "robber":
        oval(fld, p, (10.3, 0.4), (3.0, 7.0), fs=6.0)
        branch(fld, p, [(13.0, 7.0), (11.4, 3.6), (10.6, 1.4)], lw=1.3)
        branch(fld, p, [(13.0, -7.0), (14.6, -3.6), (15.2, -0.8)], lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, 15.4, 7.6, "SS comes\ndown to rob", fontsize=6.0)
        say(fld, p, 15.4, -8.4, "FS spins\nto the middle", fontsize=6.0)
    elif kind == "lurk":
        oval(fld, p, (5.6, -2.6), (3.0, 6.0), fs=6.0)
        branch(fld, p, [(1.3, -7.6), (3.4, -6.2), (5.2, -3.6)], lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, 9.6, -7.0, "W shows blitz,\ndrops out", fontsize=6.0)
    else:
        say(fld, p, 8.6, -6.2, "M blitzes:\nfive rushers", fontsize=6.0)
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 7.2))
ttl = {"rat": "1. Rat (hole player)", "robber": "2. Robber", "lurk": "3. Lurk", "rush": "4. Fifth rusher"}
for ax, kind in zip(axes.flat, ("rat", "robber", "lurk", "rush")):
    free_panel(ax, kind)
    panel_title(ax, ttl[kind])
fig.legend(handles=[LEGEND["man"], LEGEND["drop"], LEGEND["rush"], LEGEND["area"], LEGEND["ring"]],
           loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.03), ncol=5, fontsize=6.8, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4, w_pad=0.8, rect=(0, 0.04, 1, 1))
plt.show()
```

- The [**robber**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-robber) is the free defender sitting in the
  middle of the field, usually 8 to 12 yards deep, driving on in-breaking throws: digs, deep
  crossers, the slant that gets past its man. He doesn't just stare at the quarterback. In most
  teaching he keys a receiver, usually #2 or #3 to the passing strength, and "robs the first
  in-breaker", while feeling the quarterback's eyes to know when to go. Classically he is a
  safety who lines up deep (often disguised as half of a two-high shell, the subject of
  [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)) and
  comes down at the snap. His name says what he is for: he steals the throws man coverage is worst
  at defending, the ones where receivers run away from their defenders across the field. When the
  ball goes outside instead, he becomes a pursuit player: the first tackler coming from the inside.
- The [**rat**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rat) is, in many playbooks, simply another name for
  the same job. When coaches distinguish them, the rat is lower and usually a linebacker, the man
  left over when the back he would have covered stays in to block, or the Mike in the figure
  above, sitting 5 to 8 yards deep, low in the hole. (That is why the hole is sometimes called the *rat
  zone*, and the rat a *hole player*.) His prey is the shallow cross and the quarterback scramble
  up the middle.
- [**Lurk**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-lurk) describes the same idea with disguise built in.
  The lurker lines up somewhere that says something else, often walked up to the line as if
  blitzing, sometimes deep as a safety, and drops at the snap into the shallow middle. Pressure
  defenses love it, because the quarterback who sees a blitz coming throws the quick
  [hot route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) to the middle, and the lurker is standing
  in it. Some staffs use "lurk" only for a player who drops into the hole off a pressure look,
  sometimes even a defensive lineman.

Whatever it's called, the free underneath defender changes the math of Cover 1. Against pure man,
a receiver who wins inside is open. Against Cover 1 with a robber, a receiver who wins inside runs
into a second defender who has been watching the quarterback the whole time and is moving before
the ball is. Here it is in motion.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rat-dig
#| fig-cap: "Cover 1 robber against a dig, second-and-8, simulated (BDB-format tracking, generated by gridiron rather than recorded). Z runs a dig, a square break inside at about 12 yards, from the right; his cornerback, playing outside leverage, trails him across the field, as Cover 1 corners do, because the help is inside. The strong safety (SS, ringed) is the robber. Before the snap he stands 9 yards deep over the tight end Y, as if he had him in man; at the snap the Mike (M) takes Y into the flat, and the robber slides to the middle at 10 to 11 yards. Y has gone outside, so the robber looks for the next receiver coming inside: Z. When the quarterback takes his hitch step to throw the dig, the robber drives on it and arrives in the throwing lane, in front of Z, as the ball does. The free safety stays deep; the other receivers are carried by their man defenders, and because the back stays in to block, the Will (W), who had him in man, rushes through the B gap to meet him. X and his cornerback, far to the left, are out of frame. In the web version this is a video."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=-2.0), cover1_def(extra={"SS": (9.0, 8.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 5.6), "WILL": (4.5, -1.6)}),
         los=LOS, to_go=8)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.0)
route_to(p, "X", (24.0, -15.4))
route_to(p, "H", (22.0, -8.6))
route_to(p, "Y", (2.6, 10.5), (3.8, 16.5))
route_to(p, "Z", (12.0, 15.0), (12.0, 2.0), (12.4, -4.0))
p.block("RB", pts=[(0.4, -1.6)])          # the back stays in to protect
p.rush("WILL", pts=[(-3.5, -1.0), (-8.5, -1.8)], delay=0.45)   # ... so his linebacker rushes, through the B gap
T_THROW = 2.15
kf, _, _ = p._compile()
# where Z will be when a firm throw arrives, and a spot just in front of him in the lane
qb = np.array(p.position("QB", T_THROW))
t_c = T_THROW + 0.9
for _ in range(4):
    z = p.position("Z", t_c)
    t_c = T_THROW + float(np.linalg.norm(z - qb)) / 18.0
z = p.position("Z", t_c)
lane = z + (qb - z) / np.linalg.norm(qb - z) * 2.7
T_CATCH = round(t_c, 2)
# the Mike carries Y to the flat from a yard above and inside him (never dipping toward the line)
mike = [(t_, max(d_, 3.8), w_) for t_, d_, w_ in chase(p, "MIKE", "Y", off=(0.9, -1.0), lag=0.2, t_on=0.8)]
tracks = {
    "LCB": chase(p, "LCB", "X", off=(-1.0, -0.9)),
    "NB": chase(p, "NB", "H", off=(-1.0, -0.9)),
    "MIKE": mike,
    "RCB": chase(p, "RCB", "Z", off=(-1.2, 1.1), lag=0.3),
    "SS": ease([(0.0, 9.0, 8.0), (0.9, 10.2, 3.4), (T_THROW, 10.6, 2.4), (T_CATCH, *lane), (3.6, *lane)]),
    "FS": ease([(0.0, 14.0, 0.0), (1.2, 16.0, 0.6), (3.6, 16.5, 2.5)]),
}
p.pass_to("SS", t=T_THROW)      # the ball goes where the robber will be: in the lane, in front of Z
set_tracks(p, tracks, t_end=3.6)
RAT_LAT, RAT_WIN = (-11.0, 19.5), (-8.0, 19.0)
notes = ["Cover 1: a man on each receiver, FS deep.\nSS 9 yards deep over Y, as if he had him.",
         "M carries Y to the flat. SS slides to the\nmiddle, eyes on Q. Z's corner trails him.",
         "Z breaks inside on the dig and Q starts\nto throw. SS is already moving.",
         "The robber arrives in the lane in front of Z\nas the ball does: broken up or intercepted."]
if PDF:
    strip_grid(p, [0.0, 1.0, T_THROW, T_CATCH], notes, RAT_LAT, RAT_WIN, rings=[("SS", style.THIRD)],
               deco=lambda i, f, q: ruler(f, q, fs=5.5))
    plt.show()
else:
    video([p], [""], RAT_LAT, RAT_WIN, t_end=T_CATCH + 0.4, rings=[("SS", style.THIRD)], width_in=5.6)
```

The animation is simulated. If you download the 2025 Big Data Bowl files, which include the
pre-snap frames and a charted coverage for every pass play, you can watch real Cover 1 snaps the
same way; the folded code below shows how (the files are not part of this book's build).

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Cover 1 snaps from the Big Data Bowl 2025 files)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")                        # BDB 2025: 2022 season, weeks 1-9
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
# PFF's charted coverage; passResult "IN" = intercepted
cover1_picks = plays[plays["pff_passCoverage"].eq("Cover-1") & plays["passResult"].eq("IN")]
g, pl = cover1_picks.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
show_animation(bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl), times=[-1.0, 0.0, 1.2, 2.4])
```

What makes the robber work is that the dig is a *man-beater by design*. The receiver runs straight
at his defender, then breaks flat across the field, away from a corner who was protecting the
outside. Against pure man that corner is chasing, and a dig thrown on time is a completion with
room to run. The robber doesn't need to cover Z. He only needs to be in the lane when the ball
comes, which he can do because he is free to read the whole play (his key receiver and the
quarterback) instead of chasing one man. That is the key idea of
modern man coverage: **man coverage on the receivers, zone eyes on the quarterback from the one
defender who can afford them**.

The robber has his own weakness, and offenses know it. He is one man in the middle guarding a
lane, so put *two* receivers in his area at different depths, a shallow cross under a dig, and he
can only take one. That is a high-low on the robber, exactly the read
[Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) built the drive and
shallow-cross concepts around. And a quarterback who looks the robber off, staring at the middle to
pull him in before throwing outside, turns the robber's best habit against him.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden, "Cover 1" is a play on a menu, and the game decides who covers whom. On a real field
the call is a family of rules, and the most important ones are about the defender with no man.
The same Cover 1 call might have the leftover linebacker rushing if the back stays in to block,
sitting in the hole if the back releases, or spying a mobile quarterback; the safety might show
two-high and rob, or line up in the middle and stay there. The defensive coordinator also decides
technique and leverage player by player and receiver by receiver, often on the sideline between
series. Two Cover 1 calls can look nothing alike.
:::

## Cover 0: everybody's man, nobody's deep

Now remove the safety. [**Cover 0**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-0) is man coverage on
every eligible receiver with **no deep defender at all**. The "0" is the number of deep safeties.
Do the count again. The two defenders who were free in Cover 1 (the deep safety and the spare
man) have no receiver and no deep job, so they become two more rushers. Usually that doesn't mean
the safeties themselves rush: the safeties come down to cover the tight end and the back, and the
linebackers who used to cover them rush instead. So Cover 0 usually travels with a big blitz, six
or seven rushers. It is the all-out blitz, the "house call," the coverage behind the moment when
the defense decides that the quarterback won't have time to find the open man. (Not always,
though: some zero calls rush only four or five and keep one spare defender sitting low in the
middle, a "zero hole" or "zero lurk," especially near the goal line.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-cover0-empty
#| fig-cap: "Cover 0 against an empty formation (five receivers, nobody in the backfield), third-and-7. All five receivers have a man defender, each tight and shaded inside, and no one is deep: the middle of the field is open all the way to the end zone. The other six defenders rush, including both linebackers (M and W) walked up into the A gaps beside the center. Five linemen can block only five of them, so one rusher (ringed) comes free, and the quarterback has to throw before he arrives, usually in about two seconds."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -16.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -9.5),
                 O("RB", "RB", OFF_BALL, 7.6, "R"), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 11.5), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 16.5)]
dfn = zero_front() + [D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.3, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 1.5, -8.8, "$"),
                      D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.8, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 2.5, 10.9, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 3.8, 7.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=7)
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("NB", "H"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("SS", "Y"), ("FS", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)])
for k in ("WDE", "MIKE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):
    p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.7, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
p.rush("WILL", pts=[(-4.0, -0.5), (-5.0, -0.8)])
p.highlight("WILL")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-9.5, 21.5))
oval(fld, p, (15.5, 0.0), (7.0, 30.0), color=style.MUTED, label="nobody deep", alpha=0.10)
say(fld, p, -7.6, 9.0, "6 rush, 5 block:\none comes free", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -3.8, -19.6, "inside shade:\nno help anywhere", fontsize=6.8)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["man", "rush", "ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()
```

The logic is arithmetic. The offense has five linemen. If the running back and tight end go out on
routes, the five linemen are the only blockers, and six rushers beat five blockers: one is free.
If the offense keeps a back in to block, his man defender has nobody to cover. In most zero calls
he joins the rush (the "hug" rule again), so it's seven against six, still one free; in some he
just sits, as the safety does in the Corn Dog figure in
[Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd). Cover 0
is built so that **someone comes unblocked**, and the quarterback has to get rid of the ball before
he arrives. In the charted seasons, Cover 0 was played with five or more rushers about three times
in four, and the median throw against it came out about three tenths of a second sooner than
against any other coverage.[^bargain] Three tenths is roughly the difference between throwing on
the last step of the drop and taking one more hitch step to wait for a route to come open.

Because no one is behind them, Cover 0 defenders play **inside leverage**, the mirror of Cover 1.
With the linebackers rushing, nobody is left in the middle of the field, so a slant caught there
has open grass in front of it and nobody to tackle the receiver but the man chasing him. So they
take the inside throw away and dare the quarterback to throw outside, a longer, slower throw with
the sideline as an extra defender. Some teams play it *off* instead of pressed, five to seven yards
deep and inside ("zero off"), so the defenders can see the quick throw, break on it and tackle,
without the risk of being beaten clean at the line. The other danger is obvious from the picture: a receiver who beats his man on a deep
route has nothing in front of him but grass. That is the bargain.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cover0-bargain
#| fig-cap: "The Cover 0 bargain, in charted NFL dropbacks between the 20s (2023–2025 regular seasons, FTN charting). Left: the median time from snap to throw against each coverage; the Cover 0 blitz gets the ball out fastest. Right: the share of dropbacks that gained 20 yards or more; Cover 0 also gives up the most big plays, because nobody is deep. The 2018–2022 seasons (NGS charting) show the same order. Source: nflverse participation data joined to play-by-play; sacks count as dropbacks with no throw, so they are left out of the time-to-throw medians."
mid = CV[(CV["yardline_100"] > 20) & (CV["yardline_100"] < 80) & (CV["season"] >= 2023)]
order = ["COVER_0", "COVER_1", "2_MAN", "COVER_3", "COVER_2", "COVER_4", "COVER_6"]
names = {"COVER_0": "Cover 0", "COVER_1": "Cover 1", "2_MAN": "2-Man", "COVER_3": "Cover 3",
         "COVER_2": "Cover 2", "COVER_4": "Quarters (Cover 4)", "COVER_6": "Cover 6"}
g = mid.groupby("defense_coverage_type")
ttt = g["time_to_throw"].median().reindex(order)
expl = (g["explosive"].mean() * 100).reindex(order)
cols = [style.SERIES[1] if c == "COVER_0" else (style.SERIES[0] if c in ("COVER_1", "2_MAN") else style.MUTED)
        for c in order]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.1), sharey=True)
ys = np.arange(len(order))[::-1]
for ax, vals, lab, fmt in ((axes[0], ttt, "Median time to throw (seconds)", "{:.2f} s"),
                           (axes[1], expl, "Dropbacks gaining 20+ yards (%)", "{:.1f}%")):
    ax.barh(ys, vals.values, color=cols, height=0.62)
    for y_, v in zip(ys, vals.values):
        ax.text(v + vals.max() * 0.015, y_, fmt.format(v), va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_xlabel(lab, fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlim(0, vals.max() * 1.22)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
axes[0].set_yticks(ys)
axes[0].set_yticklabels([names[c] for c in order], fontsize=8)
fig.legend(handles=[Patch(color=style.SERIES[1], label="man, no deep help (Cover 0)"),
                    Patch(color=style.SERIES[0], label="other man coverages"), Patch(color=style.MUTED, label="zone")],
           fontsize=7.2, loc="upper center", ncol=3, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0))
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2, rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.92))
plt.show()
```

The chart puts numbers on the trade. Between the 20-yard lines in 2023–2025, Cover 0 got the ball
out fastest (a median of about 2.0 seconds), and it also gave up a gain of 20 yards or more on
about one dropback in seven, the highest rate of any coverage and nearly twice the rate of the
two-high zones. Cover 1, with its deep safety, sits in between. The defense is trading a higher
chance of a quick incompletion or a sack for a higher chance of a long touchdown. That is a good
bet when the offense needs a few yards and has to throw quickly anyway; it is a bad bet when one
long completion decides the game. (The full blitz menu, and how offenses protect against it, is
in [Blitzing](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd).)

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: Cover 0"}
Cover 0 exists to win a race. Every rusher it can spare is sent, so the quarterback must throw
*now*, often before his receivers have finished their routes, and every receiver has a man on him
so there is no easy hot throw. It shines where the field is short and the throw has to be quick
anyway: third-and-short, fourth down, inside the 10. **What it gives up:** any help at all. One
missed tackle, one blown assignment or one receiver who beats his man deep is a touchdown, and a
quarterback who escapes the free rusher finds a field full of defenders with their backs to him.
:::

A handful of modern coordinators have leaned on the call harder than anyone. In nflverse charting
the league leader in Cover 0 rate was Wink Martindale's Baltimore defense in 2019 and his Giants
in 2022 and 2023, and Brian Flores's Miami Dolphins in 2020 and 2021.[^zeroleaders] The most
famous is Steve Spagnuolo. His 2007 Giants beat the 18–0 Patriots in Super Bowl XLII mostly by rushing
four and blitzing only now and then, so his Cover 0 reputation comes from Kansas City, where he has been defensive
coordinator since 2019: the Chiefs ranked in the top five in Cover 0 rate in every season from 2019
to 2025, and first in 2025.[^spags] He is known less for *how often* he calls it than for *when*:
at the moments offenses least expect it, which is part of what makes it work, because a
quarterback who knows Cover 0 is coming can call a protection and a route to beat it.

## Stacks and bunches: banjo and combo coverage

Man coverage has a structural weak point, and offenses found it long ago: **receivers who line up
close together**. When two receivers stand a yard apart, or one directly behind the other in a
[stack](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stack), their defenders are close together too, and the
receivers can release in directions that make the defenders cross. A defender chasing his man has
to go around the other receiver, or around his own teammate, and loses a step. That is the
[rub](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rub-route) from
[Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd), and stacks and
[bunches](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bunch) are formations built to create it. (A rub has
to look like an accident. A receiver more than a yard past the line who deliberately blocks a
defender before the pass is thrown commits offensive pass interference, so offenses design the
two paths to cross close by, not to collide.[^opi])

The defense's answer is to stop deciding before the snap. In a
[**banjo**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-banjo), two defenders take two receivers *together*,
and decide who has whom by how the routes declare: the outside defender takes the first receiver
who breaks outside, the inside defender the first who breaks inside. Nobody has to cross anybody.
(Don't confuse it with the in-out *bracket* later in this chapter, which puts two defenders on
*one* receiver, or with the *exchange* on motion from
[Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd), which
swaps receivers before the snap.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-banjo
#| fig-cap: "The same stack release against two ways of covering it (the offense's right side, with the sideline at the right edge; simulated). Z is on the line, H directly behind him. Z runs a slant inside, H a quick out. Top row, locked man: the cornerback (CB) has Z and the nickel ($) has H, so they have to cross each other and H's release; both lose ground in the traffic and both receivers come open (the yards are each receiver's separation from his defender). Bottom row, banjo: the same two defenders wait for the routes to declare; the cornerback, outside, takes the receiver who breaks out (H) and the nickel, inside, takes the one who breaks in (Z). Nobody crosses, and both receivers are covered. In the web version this is a video."
BJ_LAT, BJ_WIN = (4.0, 28.2), (-4.0, 12.0)


def stack_play():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 13.0), O("H", "WR", -2.6, 13.6)]
    dfn = [D("RCB", "CB", 4.8, 15.8, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 4.8, 10.4, "$")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    route_to(p, "Z", (2.0, 13.0), (6.0, 8.5), (7.6, 6.4))
    route_to(p, "H", (2.4, 14.1), (4.4, 19.6), (4.7, 21.2))
    return p


lock, banjo = stack_play(), stack_play()
set_tracks(lock, {   # each has to cross the other and H's release: both lose ground in the traffic
    "RCB": ease([(0.0, 4.8, 15.8), (0.6, 3.0, 14.9), (1.0, 3.7, 13.2), (1.45, 5.2, 10.6), (2.0, 6.2, 8.2)]),
    "NB": ease([(0.0, 4.8, 10.4), (0.6, 5.4, 12.4), (1.0, 4.6, 14.4), (1.45, 4.6, 16.6), (2.0, 4.8, 18.6)]),
}, t_end=2.0)
set_tracks(banjo, {  # they wait for the routes to declare, then take the receiver who comes to their side
    "RCB": ease([(0.0, 4.8, 15.8), (0.6, 4.6, 16.0), (1.0, 4.6, 17.4), (1.45, 5.1, 20.3), (2.0, 5.3, 21.6)]),
    "NB": ease([(0.0, 4.8, 10.4), (0.6, 5.1, 9.8), (1.07, 5.8, 7.8), (1.45, 7.8, 6.0), (2.0, 8.0, 5.6)]),
}, t_end=2.0)
BJ_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.45]
PAIRS = {0: (("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H")), 1: (("RCB", "H"), ("NB", "Z"))}


def banjo_deco(i, j, fld, p):
    """Sideline cue in every panel; each receiver's separation from his defender in the last column."""
    say(fld, p, -2.4, 22.6, "outside →", fontsize=6.0)
    if j == len(BJ_T) - 1:
        for dk, rk in PAIRS[i]:
            sep = float(np.linalg.norm(np.array(p.position(dk, BJ_T[j])) - np.array(p.position(rk, BJ_T[j]))))
            rd, rw = p.position(rk, BJ_T[j])
            txt = f"{sep:.0f} yd: open" if sep >= 1.6 else f"{max(sep, 1.0):.0f} yd: covered"
            say(fld, p, rd + 1.9, rw, txt, fontsize=5.8, color=OD if sep >= 1.6 else DD, weight="bold")


if PDF:
    strip_rows([lock, banjo], ["Locked man", "Banjo"], BJ_T,
               [["CB has Z, $ has H.", "They must cross: traffic.", "Both receivers open."],
                ["They wait for the routes.", "Z breaks in, H out.", "CB takes H, $ takes Z."]],
               BJ_LAT, BJ_WIN, deco=banjo_deco)
    plt.show()
else:
    video([lock, banjo], ["Locked man", "Banjo"], BJ_LAT, BJ_WIN, t_end=1.8, width_in=6.4)
```

Notice where the banjo defenders stand: about five yards off, not pressed. They need a moment to
see which way each receiver is going, and from the line of scrimmage they would have no time to
read before having to commit. The in/out split is the most common; some teams split them
*low/high* instead, so the first receiver to break short goes to one defender and the first to
go deep to the other. Every banjo also needs a rule for the release that doesn't declare neatly,
both receivers going the same way or both running straight upfield; usually the defenders fall
back on their pre-snap match, or the outside man takes #1.

The banjo solves the rub by trading a little of man coverage's certainty for zone-like
flexibility. It is a small zone rule inside a man call: for the first yard or two, each defender
guards a *side* rather than a person, then locks on to whoever comes to that side. (It runs the
opposite way from the [pattern matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pattern-matching) you
met in Coverage Fundamentals, which is a *zone* call whose defenders become man defenders once the
routes declare. A banjo starts from man and borrows a moment of zone.) That makes it the simplest
example of a [**combo coverage**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-combo-coverage), the general
name for coverages in which two or more defenders share receivers and decide who takes whom by
how the routes declare. Against a three-receiver bunch, a common version is a **"point" call**:
one defender presses the receiver at the point of the bunch (the one nearest the line), and the
other two play first-out and first-in on the other two. Bigger combos play man on one side of the
formation and zone on the other.

The price is communication and a new weakness. Both defenders must call it, both must read the
same release, and both must commit at the same instant. Offenses go after banjos with routes that
make the release ambiguous. The clearest is to send both receivers the same way, one a beat
after the other.

```{python}
#| label: fig-banjo-beater
#| fig-cap: "How an offense beats a banjo (the same stack and the same two defenders; illustrative). Both receivers break inside, one a beat after the other. Z runs a quick slant (1), the first receiver inside, so the nickel ($), the inside defender, takes him. H pushes upfield and breaks inside a beat later (2) on a short in-cut. Nobody has broken outside, so the cornerback's man is H, but H is now running away from him across the field with a two-to-three-yard head start, the very traffic problem the banjo was meant to avoid."
p = Play(line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 13.0), O("H", "WR", -2.6, 13.6)],
         [D("RCB", "CB", 4.8, 15.8, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 4.8, 10.4, "$")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p, "Z", (1.6, 13.0), (4.4, 9.0), (5.0, 7.2))          # first inside: quick slant
route_to(p, "H", (2.4, 14.0), (7.8, 14.3), (8.0, 5.6))         # second inside, a beat later
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-4.8, 28.2), window=(-6.8, 12.5))
branch(fld, p, [(4.8, 10.4), (4.7, 9.3), (5.6, 7.9)])                  # $ takes the first in-breaker
branch(fld, p, [(4.8, 15.8), (5.8, 15.7), (7.2, 13.6), (7.4, 11.4)])   # CB chases the second, from behind
say(fld, p, 2.0, 6.0, "1. Z in first:\n$ takes him", fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, 10.6, 10.6, "2. H in, a beat later: the CB\nmust chase him across, behind", fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, -2.4, 22.6, "outside →", fontsize=6.4)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["route", "react"])
plt.show()
```

Other counters work the same way: a receiver who fakes in and breaks back out after the
defenders have committed (the [whip](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-whip) from
[Passing Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)), or a third receiver
arriving in the space the two defenders vacated. That is why bunch formations are a red-zone
staple, and the red zone, as the numbers later in this chapter show, is where man coverage is most
common. Bunches stress whatever rule the defense has.

The charters who label coverages for the NFL's public data see these mixtures too. From 2023 on,
the charting used by nflverse includes a label, COMBO, for plays that don't fit a single coverage
name. The data dictionary lists COMBO without defining it, so it is safest to read it as "a
mixture the charter didn't force into one box"; this chapter's counts leave those plays out.

## Brackets: two on one

Sometimes the problem isn't the formation; it's one receiver. The offense has a player the defense
cannot cover one-on-one, and leaving him in man coverage, even with a deep safety somewhere, is
asking for a long afternoon. The answer is a [**bracket**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bracket):
two defenders on one receiver, one on each side of him, so whichever way he breaks, somebody is
already there.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bracket-3x1
#| fig-cap: "A bracket on the isolated receiver in a 3x1 formation. The offense puts its best receiver, X (ringed), alone on the left as #1, with three receivers to the right. The defense brackets him: the left cornerback presses a step inside X and plays underneath, in trail technique, and the free safety (FS) plays over the top, 12 yards deep and only about 4 yards inside X, far from the middle of the field. The trips side is man coverage, with the strong safety (SS) as the single deep defender over it. The cost shows in the middle: the safety who would have been the robber is spent on X, so nobody sits in the hole, and the trips side's man defenders have only one safety behind them."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.0, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 7.5),
                 O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 17.0)]
dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 6.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"),
```
